units.title: The benchmark question, its decision owner and an immutable manifest
outcomes: Turn a serving benchmark into a decision with an owner, two alternatives and a reversal condition.
Extend your experiment manifest to bind request semantics, quality, failures and cost to each result.
Separate tuning traffic from a frozen final evaluation corpus before selecting configurations.
units.why: Build on Manifests, claim schemas, predictions declared first and artifact lineage. The new contract must support a serving decision, not just reproduce a device timing.

next.note: Choose counters that answer the declared decision.

study.title: The optimization plan before the benchmark
study.locator: Chapter 9, LLM Serving Optimization Plan, printed pp. 294 to 296; Step 2: Generate Benchmark Traffic, pp. 297 to 300
study.depth: Read the workflow, not the hardware setup commands. Replace the worked model and deployment with a small model that fits your GPU; keep distributed variants as reading.

study.title: Bind experiments to their serving contract
study.locator: Core requirements: recorded workload corpus; Architecture constraints: versions, tuning versus final traces and hardware tier; Milestone C: hypothesis and reversal conditions

focus: Name the decision owner and the action the evidence can change: retain the baseline, enable the contribution or add capacity. Set correctness and SLO gates before tuning.
Bind model, tokenizer, template, adapter, weight and KV precision, engine revision, effective configuration, hardware state and workload hashes to the run.
Retain intended arrival times, output limits, stop rules, tenant scope, deadlines, retry policy and quality evaluator. A prompt list alone is not a workload.
Split by sessions or shared-prefix groups where leakage is possible. Freeze final traces and transformations before configuration selection.
units.reproduce: Without notes, write a decision record and manifest for your existing `servelab` baseline. Give each tuning and final corpus a digest. Change the output stop rule in a second record and verify that the workload identity changes rather than silently reusing the first result.
traps: A package version does not identify a locally patched engine. Record the source revision and patch digest too.
Selecting a configuration after inspecting final traces turns them into tuning data. Acquire a new final set before making a generalization claim.
Calling synthetic prefix repetition representative of demand. It isolates reuse; it does not supply production arrival or length distributions.

selfTest.q: What makes a benchmark question actionable?
selfTest.a: An owner, a choice between alternatives, fixed correctness and SLO constraints, and an observation that would reverse the choice.

selfTest.q: Why is freezing prompts insufficient?
selfTest.a: Tokenization, arrivals, output lengths, stopping, cache state, retries and evaluation can change the work even when prompt text stays fixed.

selfTest.q: May the final workload use the same length distribution as tuning?
selfTest.a: Yes. The distributions can match, but final requests or sessions must not have been used to select the configuration. Record any intended distribution shift separately.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` decision record, immutable experiment manifests and separate tuning and final traces.
units.stopWhen: Your decision record names two alternatives and a reversal condition, and a changed request contract cannot reuse an old manifest identity.

fit.note: The Chapter 9 workflow and capstone constraints cover governance and corpus separation; the mini-project supplies manifest implementation.

units.title: Offered and completed load, goodput and useful work
outcomes: Reconcile offered, admitted, completed, failed and pending work from one trace boundary.
Compute request and token goodput under a fixed quality and latency contract.
Explain a utilization increase that does not increase useful completed work.
units.why: Build on Benchmark scenarios, MLPerf boundaries and endpoint goodput. Here you audit the engine's accounting and use it to locate sustainable serving capacity.

next.note: Price useful outputs instead of gross token activity.

study.title: Audit throughput and the traffic boundary
study.locator: Chapter 9, Step 3: Define Evaluation Metrics, printed pp. 300 to 301; Step 5: Benchmark the Qwen3 Model with vLLM, pp. 302 to 303
study.depth: Use the two workload reports as accounting examples, not a controlled cache ablation: their length distributions and request rates differ. Do not infer cache benefit from their total-token throughput ratio.

study.title: Capacity subject to per-request service quality
study.locator: arXiv:2407.07000v2, Sections 2.2, 3.1 and 4.2: metric boundaries, hidden stalls and Capacity Evaluation

focus: Use the same observation interval for rates. Also report an arrival cohort followed to terminal outcomes; a drain interval must not be silently counted as offered-load time.
Define request goodput as quality-accepted completions satisfying all declared request SLOs per second. Token goodput counts only the accepted outputs of those requests, using one tokenizer.
Capacity is a sustainable offered rate satisfying the target success fraction without persistent queue growth. It is not the maximum observed completion rate during a drain.
Device busy time, padding, recomputation and rejected output can increase utilization without increasing useful work. Use correlated request and iteration traces to distinguish them.
units.reproduce: Recount one `servelab` trace closed-book. For a CPU-checkable fixture, offer 100 unique requests in 10 seconds with no initial queue: 70 succeed, 10 fail, 10 are rejected and 10 remain pending at the boundary. Of the successes, 50 pass both quality and SLO gates and each returns 20 accepted output tokens. Obtain 10 offered requests/s, 7 successful completions/s, 5 good requests/s and 100 good output tokens/s; account for every request once.
traps: Calling the configured request rate the actual offered rate when client concurrency limits delay sending. Retain intended and actual send times.
Counting cached input tokens as executed prefill work. Logical input throughput and computed-token throughput need separate counters.
Dropping timeouts from the denominator. They are demand and service failures, not missing observations.

selfTest.q: Can completed load briefly exceed offered load?
selfTest.a: Yes, when an earlier backlog drains. Report the initial and final backlog and use a common time boundary.

selfTest.q: Does higher device utilization prove a useful throughput gain?
selfTest.a: No. Padding, retries or recomputation can keep the device busy. Valid accepted completions and their SLOs determine useful work.

selfTest.q: Is request goodput multiplied by mean output length always token goodput?
selfTest.a: Only if that mean is taken over the same good requests with the same tokenizer and interval. A mean over all completions can give a different value.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` raw-outcome reconciliation and offered-load sweep with quality- and SLO-aware goodput.
units.stopWhen: Every offered request is accounted for, and you identify a sustainable load point from success fraction, goodput and queue growth rather than utilization alone.

fit.note: Chapter 9 supplies accounting examples and Etalon supplies the constrained capacity workflow; the mini-project supplies measurement and reconciliation.

units.title: Cost per token, quality acceptance, retry cost and energy
outcomes: Derive input, output and quality-accepted output unit costs with explicit allocation rules.
Account for failed attempts, retries, idle capacity and failure reserve in serving cost.
Optionally derive joules and operational carbon per useful output with an explicit measurement boundary.
units.why: Build on Unit cost, headroom and simpler designs. Token counts now need quality, retry and allocation rules before they can support an economic comparison.

next.note: Carry attempt cost and useful-output rates into the capacity plan.

study.locator: Inference at Scale, Serving cost can dominate training cost: Napkin Math 1.1 and equation 2; The serving hierarchy
study.depth: Stop before Serving Architecture Dimensions. Treat the monetary examples as assumed scenarios, not current prices or measurements.

study.title: Quality, retries and cost belong to one planner
study.locator: Core requirements: analytical planner; Architecture constraints: correctness and quality; Failure-injection requirements: retry storm; Measurement requirements: quality and cost/token/request

study.title: Optional energy and operational carbon boundary
study.locator: Energy measurement techniques: Hardware power counters and System-level energy profiling; Carbon Footprint Calculation: Operational carbon calculation, equation 11
study.depth: Optional: read the measurement and unit-conversion method only. Do not adopt the chapter's hardware power estimates or fleet results.

focus: For total interval cost \(C\), report \(C/N_{\text{in}}\), \(C/N_{\text{out}}\) and \(C/N_{\text{accepted}}\) as separate normalizations, not additive charges. Splitting input and output charges requires an explicit allocation policy.
Sum costs over every attempt for a logical request; count its accepted output once. Retry amplification depends on failure correlation, backoff, deadline and attempt cap.
Keep quality acceptance separate from speculative draft-token acceptance. A verified draft token is not evidence that an answer meets the application's quality gate.
Optional: integrate measured power over the same interval as accepted work. GPU energy alone is not total IT energy; facility overhead and grid intensity are assumptions unless measured.
units.reproduce: Derive a synthetic accounting example without notes: an interval costs 12 currency units, processes 6000 input tokens and generates 3000 output tokens across all attempts, of which 2000 are quality-accepted useful output tokens. Obtain 0.002 per input token, 0.004 per generated output token and 0.006 per accepted token. With independent attempts of constant cost \(c\), success probability \(p\) and unlimited retries, derive expected cost \(c/p\); state why bounded deadlines and correlated failures require a different model. Optional: a constant 100 W over 10 seconds is 1000 J, or 0.5 J per accepted token for this fixture.
traps: Dividing only successful-attempt cost by accepted output. Failed attempts and provisioned idle time still consume budget.
Comparing token costs across tokenizers as if tokens were identical work. Use the same text tasks and quality gate; report tokenizer identity.
Applying facility overhead twice or to GPU energy alone and calling it a measured facility footprint. State what is missing.

selfTest.q: May input-normalized and output-normalized total costs be added?
selfTest.a: No. Each uses the same numerator. Adding them double counts cost; additive input/output prices need an allocation or billing rule.

selfTest.q: When does expected retry cost equal \(c/p\)?
selfTest.a: For independent, identically distributed attempts, constant per-attempt cost, positive success probability and unlimited retries. Deadline caps and correlated failures invalidate that shortcut.

selfTest.q: What if no output passes the quality gate?
selfTest.a: Cost per accepted token has no finite value. Report zero accepted output and the spent cost; do not replace the denominator with generated tokens.

selfTest.q: How do you convert energy to operational carbon?
selfTest.a: Multiply facility energy in kWh by the corresponding grid intensity in mass per kWh. Apply facility overhead once if starting from complete IT energy; report embodied carbon separately.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` attempt-cost ledger and quality-accepted output denominator, with optional energy/carbon accounting.
units.stopWhen: Your cost table reconciles all attempts and idle/reserve charges, counts accepted work once and states the units and allocation boundary of every denominator.

fit.note: The selected economics reading lacks optional energy/carbon accounting; Sustainable AI adds verified measurement and carbon subsections. The capstone planner supplies retry and quality practice.

units.title: Fair warmup and arrivals, raw traces and tail percentiles with uncertainty

Regenerate latency and goodput summaries from raw per-request records, including failures.
Report p50, p95 and p99 with uncertainty that respects trial or session dependence.

next.note: Use the trial contract for contribution comparisons.

study.title: Benchmark state and endpoint boundary
study.locator: Page read 2026-10-14, generated from commit cc63e66: Before Benchmarking; Preparing a Dataset; Online Serving Benchmarking; Startup Metrics

study.title: Retain the request evidence and observer control
study.locator: Milestone B: correlated events, observer overhead, raw timestamps and decode gaps; Milestone E: open-loop final workloads

study.title: Resampling independent experimental units
study.locator: Opening resampling procedure; Parameters: statistic, paired, method and rng; Notes: degenerate data; Examples: difference between means and paired-sample statistics
study.depth: Skip plotting and Array API support. Use the procedure on independent replay trials or justified blocks, not on individual dependent tokens.

focus: Warmup ends at a declared readiness condition. Reset or prepopulate caches identically according to the experiment question; cold cache and cold model startup are different states.
Randomize off/on order within replay pairs. Keep intended arrivals fixed, record actual sends and retain client delays so a concurrency cap cannot conceal overload.

Keep arrival, admission, first-content, stream-chunk, completion and terminal-error records with token counts and request identity. Client chunk timestamps are not necessarily individual token timestamps.

Declare the quantile estimator and the population: request TTFT, request TPOT or token gaps. Resample whole independent trial pairs, recomputing the chosen statistic; report sample counts and sparse-tail limitations.
units.reproduce: Without notes, reconstruct p50, p95 and p99 and goodput from one stored replay, stating clock and timing boundaries. Then resample independent off/on trial pairs with replacement and recompute the difference in the chosen percentile for each resample. Keep the same pair indices for both variants. Save the seed, quantile method and resampling unit; demonstrate that duplicating a request identifier causes your reconciliation check to fail.
traps: Computing percentiles of batch means and calling them request percentiles. Aggregation has changed the population.
Using more bootstrap resamples to compensate for too few tail observations. Resampling cannot invent an unseen tail.
Filtering failed requests and presenting the remaining latency distribution as all-user service quality. Report failures and censoring alongside successful latencies.

selfTest.q: Why preserve off/on pairing during resampling?
selfTest.a: The pair shares replay conditions. Breaking it discards that dependence and changes the uncertainty of the difference.

selfTest.q: Is the average of trial p99 values the pooled request p99?
selfTest.a: No. Quantiles are nonlinear. Pool raw observations to estimate pooled p99, or explicitly report the mean of trial p99 values as a different statistic.

selfTest.q: Why not independently resample every token gap?
selfTest.a: Gaps share requests, scheduler iterations and cache state. Independent resampling can understate uncertainty; use trials or justified dependent blocks.

selfTest.q: Does a narrow interval from a tiny sample establish p99 precisely?
selfTest.a: No. Tail coverage may be poor or the bootstrap degenerate. Report the observation count and limitation, and collect more independent evidence.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` paired replay campaign, retained raw traces and percentile/uncertainty transformations.
units.stopWhen: A fresh analysis run regenerates your percentile and goodput tables from raw records, and your report justifies cache controls, sampling units and tail uncertainty.

fit.note: The pool covers trial governance and raw traces but lacks a worked uncertainty procedure; SciPy adds verified resampling examples, with trial-level application in the mini-project.

units.title: Capacity headroom under demand growth across three scenarios
outcomes: Derive a capacity and cost plan for three workload/SLO scenarios using measured replica capacity.
Budget demand growth, retries, quality acceptance, startup lag and a stated failure reserve.
Identify which fleet assumptions remain analytical rather than validated by a single-device run.
units.why: The serving planner extends Unit cost, headroom and simpler designs with a measured SLO boundary. A token-rate peak is not a safe provisioning point.

next.note: Reprice the plan after measuring the contribution's boundary.

study.title: Choose the constraint before the topology
study.locator: When single-machine serving is insufficient, Table 1 and Checkpoint 1.1; The serving tax: Overhead of distribution, equation 1; Serving cost can dominate training cost, equation 2

study.title: Find capacity under the declared SLO
study.locator: arXiv:2407.07000v2, Section 4.2: Capacity Evaluation; Section 5.2: Evaluating Open Source Systems
study.depth: Use the load-search method, not the paper's hardware capacities. Keep your SLO common across compared systems.

study.title: The scenario and failure planner
study.locator: Core requirements: analytical planner; Hardware variants; Measurement requirements: capacity headroom; Design-defense questions 5, 7 and 10

focus: Use three declared scenarios: interactive short prompts with a strict first-token target; long-context summarization; and bursty shared-prefix traffic with cancellations. Preserve their joint length/reuse distributions, not just means.

Let \(q_s\) be sustainable attempts/s per healthy replica for scenario \(s\), and \(h_s\) the fraction deliberately left unused. Under balanced identical replicas, require \((n-f)(1-h_s)q_s \geq \lambda_s a_s\), where \(f\) is failed replicas, \(\lambda_s\) logical requests/s and \(a_s\) expected attempts/request.
Quality and SLO acceptance convert served attempts into useful outcomes. Do not divide demand by acceptance unless the product actually retries rejected answers; model that retry policy explicitly.

Sweep growth and a major failure separately. Include startup lag, cold-cache recovery, routing imbalance and reserve charges; the replica inequality is an analytical starting point, not a fleet latency proof.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the replica inequality and apply it to a labeled analytical fixture: balanced identical replicas each sustain 10 attempts/s; reserve 20% of that rate, allow one failed replica, demand 24 logical requests/s and assume 1.25 attempts/request. Obtain five provisioned replicas. At 10x demand obtain 39. Then build the three-scenario table from your own measured capacity points, with fleet routing and failures checked in a labeled CPU simulation.
traps: Adding another utilization discount to a capacity number already defined at that same utilization target. State what reserve is additional.
Multiplying single-replica capacity by replica count without cache skew, imbalance or fault-domain assumptions.
Budgeting steady-state capacity while ignoring backlog during model startup and cold-cache recovery.

selfTest.q: Why does the fixture need five replicas rather than four?
selfTest.a: Demand is 30 attempts/s. Four healthy replicas at 8 attempts/s each suffice, but one additional replica is needed to preserve that capacity after one failure.

selfTest.q: Does sharding always improve a strict latency scenario?
selfTest.a: No. It adds communication and coordination. Derive those costs and distinguish single-request execution from queueing before choosing it.

selfTest.q: Can three scenarios share one measured capacity constant?
selfTest.a: Only with evidence that their service and SLO boundaries match. Length, reuse, bursts and stopping commonly change sustainable capacity.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` three-scenario capacity/cost planner, 10x growth sensitivity and simulated failure reserve.
units.stopWhen: Each scenario has a measured single-replica SLO point, a derived growth/failure plan and a cost table whose fleet assumptions are explicitly labeled.

fit.note: The opening architecture/economics analysis, Etalon capacity search and capstone planner extend prior headroom arithmetic to three serving scenarios.

units.title: Reconstructing the engine API, tokenizer path, scheduler and request state
outcomes: Map API validation, templating, tokenization and request identity into exact source owners.
Reconstruct scheduler state transitions and the iteration work order without relying on class names alone.
Predict where Nano-vLLM responsibilities move in Mini-SGLang and vLLM V1.

study.locator: System Architecture: Key Components and Data Flow; Code Organization: server, tokenizer, message and scheduler modules; follow `python/minisgl/scheduler/scheduler.py`, `_process_one_msg` and `_schedule_next_batch`

study.title: The production scheduling work order
study.locator: Chapter 8, Generation-Request Execution Workflow and Scheduler Deep Dive, printed pp. 278 to 284
study.depth: Treat the prose as an architecture sketch, not a fairness guarantee. Use vLLM 0.31.0 source to resolve implementation details.

study.title: vLLM 0.31.0 process and input boundaries
study.locator: V1 Process Architecture: API Server Process and Engine Core Process; compare `vllm/v1/engine/input_processor.py`, `vllm/v1/request.py` and `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` in release 0.31.0
study.depth: Skip the later AsyncLLMEngine description as a V1 implementation guide. In release 0.31.0, the launcher imports `AsyncLLM` from `vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py`; the older name is a compatibility alias.

focus: Reuse your earlier request-state invariants. For every arrow, record caller, callee, process, message payload, request ID and owner of terminal cleanup.
Nano-vLLM accepts token IDs or text but supplies no HTTP frontend. Mini-SGLang adds API, tokenizer and scheduler messages; API schema fields still need tracing to implementation.
At the pinned Nano-vLLM commit, the scheduler returns a prefill batch before considering decode if prefill work was scheduled. Chunked prefill alone therefore does not prove decode protection.
Compare the miniature phase flag with V1's token-progress scheduling. Identify admission and preemption decisions separately from batch tensor preparation.
units.reproduce: Draw the three frontend-to-scheduler maps without notes. Annotate a short request, a chunked long prompt and a preempted request with state owner and token progress. Replay these transitions on CPU with your existing deterministic scheduler and check resource and request invariants; keep differences from the pinned engine explicit rather than claiming simulation is execution evidence.
traps: Assuming matching class names mean matching process boundaries or scheduling policy across engines.
Reading only normal completion. Preemption can return a running request to waiting with a different cache state.
Treating continuous batching as bounded fairness. Demonstrate bounded wait under the actual arrivals and admission policy.

selfTest.q: Why trace a supported API field past validation?
selfTest.a: A schema can accept a field that is not forwarded or implemented. The actual request contract is determined by the whole path.

selfTest.q: Does Nano-vLLM's chunked prefill automatically interleave decode?
selfTest.a: Not at the pinned commit. `schedule` returns scheduled prefill work before the decode loop; arrivals can keep prefill taking precedence.

selfTest.q: Which component should own the batch tensor layout?
selfTest.a: The runner or its preparation layer. The scheduler determines feasible token work and ownership metadata; the runner translates that plan into execution inputs. Verify the actual split in source.

outcomes: Trace logical token positions through cache lookup, physical allocation and runner metadata to attention dispatch.

Explain which runner assumptions constrain a scheduler or cache contribution.

study.locator: `can_allocate`, `allocate`, `deallocate`, `may_append` and `hash_blocks`; follow `nanovllm/engine/model_runner.py`: `allocate_kv_cache`, `prepare_prefill`, `prepare_decode` and `run_model`; then `nanovllm/layers/attention.py`: `Attention.forward`

study.locator: `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks`, `allocate_slots` and `free`; follow `vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py`: `_prepare_inputs`, `_build_attention_metadata`, `execute_model` and `initialize_attn_backend`
study.depth: Trace one supported dense text model and selected backend. Hybrid cache groups and distributed connectors are interface reading, not an implementation requirement.

focus: Record the cache key, lookup result, references, free/used accounting and invalidation scope. Equal prompt suffixes are not equal prefixes.
Separate cache storage from attention addressing. The allocator chooses physical pages; the runner supplies positions, lengths, slot mappings and block tables; the backend consumes them.
Nano-vLLM excludes the final prompt block from prefix lookup at this commit. Follow the exact recomputed suffix rather than assuming every complete prompt block is reused.
Graph replay, padding and asynchronously prepared metadata extend lifetimes. A free operation must respect in-flight consumers, not merely the host request status.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map a cold prompt, an exact shared prefix and an append across a page boundary from request tokens to attention inputs. Use a CPU page-table fixture to compare gathered logical KV with a contiguous oracle and to recount references after release. Annotate the corresponding pinned source calls and graph/eager dispatch boundary; inspect GPU execution separately from this address-correctness check.
traps: Calling an unreferenced cached page unused memory. It may remain reusable until eviction; release and eviction are different operations.
Assuming a cache hash supplies model, tokenizer and tenant isolation. Verify the full identity scope separately.
Treating Mini-SGLang's `check_integrity` as a complete invariant suite. It is an empty method in the pinned radix implementation; write independent checks.

selfTest.q: Which two maps are needed to find a cached token's physical KV?
selfTest.a: The request's logical token position to logical page/offset, and its block table from logical page to physical page. Layer and KV-head layout then locate the values.

selfTest.q: Why can released KV still occupy cache storage?
selfTest.a: Release removes active references, but a prefix index may retain reusable content. Eviction makes that storage available for replacement.

selfTest.q: Does a prefix hit prove the runner skips the whole prompt?
selfTest.a: No. Lookup rules, block alignment and the need to recompute a final token or suffix determine actual skipped work. Trace returned token counts and scheduled inputs.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` cache/runner source map and CPU logical-to-physical KV oracle checks.

study.depth: Worker/rank coordination is source reading plus labeled local-process simulation. Trace actual execution with one worker on your GPU; additional GPUs are not required.

focus: Mark when sampled token IDs become request state, when text becomes printable, when a chunk is sent and when the client sees content. These are distinct timing boundaries.
Follow cancellation past the frontend acknowledgment. Request queues, KV references, in-flight work and output collectors may have different cleanup times.
Mini-SGLang's overlap loop can observe terminal requests again while earlier work completes. Its finished-request guard is an ownership clue, not a reason to remove duplicate-event tests.
Locate each telemetry producer and aggregation boundary. Join request and iteration records without logging sensitive prompt text or introducing unbounded metric labels.
units.reproduce: Without notes, draw successful completion and cancellation during an in-flight iteration through all output and cleanup owners. Use CPU fake-runner events to replay late output after cancellation and repeated terminal notifications; assert no second client completion and no double release. Link each event to the pinned implementation and identify the telemetry needed to distinguish generated tokens from client-visible content.
traps: Equating one stream chunk with one model token. Detokenization, buffering and output intervals can merge or delay content.
Using Nano-vLLM's terminal batch output as proof of online streaming behavior. That interface returns completed outputs, not an HTTP stream.
Trusting Mini-SGLang's non-streaming usage fields as measured counts. The pinned API returns literal zeros there; count token IDs independently.

selfTest.q: Does receiving an abort acknowledgment prove all KV is reusable immediately?
selfTest.a: No. Follow the cache owner and any in-flight consumers to the safe release point; acknowledgment and device completion can differ.

selfTest.q: Why can first-content latency exceed first sampled-token latency?
selfTest.a: A token may not yet decode to printable text, and output processing, buffering, transport or a slow client can delay visible content.

selfTest.q: What can a CPU worker-loss simulation establish?
selfTest.a: Request identity, terminal outcome, retry and bounded cleanup behavior under its event model. It cannot establish collective timing or distributed GPU throughput.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the `servelab` output/worker/telemetry map and CPU cancellation, late-output and duplicate-terminal replay checks.
units.stopWhen: Your map distinguishes generated tokens, visible chunks and safe release, and both normal completion and cancellation reconcile every owner and telemetry record.
